alignment.note: Both Greek (καί) and Vulgate (Et) open with the connective conjunction; the Peshitta omits the introductory copula entirely, beginning paratactically with the verb ܐܡܪ, a stylistic feature of Syriac narrative which does not require an opening conjunction here.

Greek ἔλεγεν and Latin dicebat are both imperfect, conveying durative/iterative speech ('he kept saying'); the Peshitta ܐܡܪ is a simple perfect, flattening the aspectual nuance to a punctual 'he said'.
αὐτοῖς / ܠܗܘܢ / illis ('to them'); the Vulgate's colon (index 3) is included as the punctuation introducing the direct discourse.

Greek ἀθετεῖτε ('you set aside, nullify') is rendered analytically: the Peshitta uses participle ܛܠܡܝܢ plus explicit pronoun ܐܢܬܘܢ ('you do injustice to / reject'), drawing on the root ṭ-l-m connoting wronging or oppressing, while the Vulgate uses the periphrasis irritum facitis ('you make void'). All converge on the sense of annulment, but the Syriac introduces a connotation of injustice absent from the Greek and Latin.
τοῦ θεοῦ / ܕܐܠܗܐ / Dei ('of God'); the Vulgate comma after Dei is part of this token.
Purpose conjunction ἵνα / Syriac prefixed ܕ- (within ܕܬܩܝܡܘܢ) / ut ('that, so that').

Greek στήσητε ('that you may establish/maintain', from ἵστημι) and Latin servetis ('that you may keep') stand at clause-end, while the Syriac fuses the conjunction and verb into ܕܬܩܝܡܘܢ (root q-m, 'establish') in clause-initial position, reflecting the verb-first tendency of Syriac syntax.

The possessive 'your' is an independent genitive pronoun in Greek (ὑμῶν) and Latin (vestram), but in Syriac it is expressed as the enclitic suffix -ܟܘܢ attached to ܡܫܠܡܢܘܬܟܘܢ, so the noun and possessive share a single token.
